tier_reason: The FAST'18 paper compares FAST+FAIR with wB+-tree, FP-tree, WORT and SkipList (plus B-link tree for concurrency) and states g++ 4.8.2 -O3 and the Xeon E7-4809 v3. It is not tier A because the DICL/FAST_FAIR repo holds only the FAST+FAIR code (single/, concurrent/, *_pmdk/ test programs) with no wB+-tree, FP-tree, WORT, SkipList or B-link implementations, so the published benchmark code does not run against the named baselines; that makes it a peer-reviewed B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: FAST'18 paper: range queries up to 20x faster than SkipList and 6-27% faster than FP-tree / 25-33% faster than wB+-tree (10M 8-byte random keys, 1KB nodes, 300ns PM read latency). Insertion: FAST+FAIR, FP-tree and WORT are comparable and beat wB+-tree and SkipList 'by a large margin' (wB+-tree issues 1.7x more cache-line flushes); as PM write latency rises FAST+FAIR consistently outperforms FP-tree, wB+-tree and SkipList, but WORT is fastest. The 'up to 1.61x faster than wB+-tree' figure is from the ARM (Nexus 5 / Snapdragon 800) non-TSO insertion experiment, not the Xeon runs. TPC-C mixes W1-W4: FAST+FAIR consistently outperforms the other indexes (figure only, no ratio). Concurrency is self-scaling only: search throughput rises about 11.7x from 1 to 16 threads, insertion about 12.5x at 16 threads (FP-tree 7.7x, B-link 4.4x), and the mixed workload reaches up to 11.44x the single-thread throughput. The '~2.2x higher than B-link tree at 8 threads' figure belongs to FP-tree (TSX), not FAST+FAIR.
corrections.baseline: wB+-tree, FP-tree, WORT and SkipList (single-threaded); FP-tree, B-link tree and SkipList (concurrent)
corrections.hardware: Workstation with two Intel Xeon Haswell-EX E7-4809 v3 @ 2.0GHz (16 vCPUs with hyper-threading, 20MB L3), 64GB DDR3 DRAM; threads bound to one socket with numactl for the concurrent runs; PM latency emulated with the Quartz DRAM-based emulator. The ARM experiment ran on a Nexus 5 (Snapdragon 800 @ 2.26GHz) with nop-injected PM write latency.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 118 stars; evaluated as a baseline in later persistent-memory index papers including DPTree (PVLDB 13(4)) and APEX (VLDB'22). The LB+-Tree (PVLDB 13(7)) and BzTree (PVLDB 11(5)) papers do not evaluate it.
corrections.caveats: PM was emulated (Quartz on DRAM; nop injection on ARM), not real Optane. FAST+FAIR is not uniformly fastest: WORT wins insertion at higher PM write latency; FP-tree searches slightly faster when read latency exceeds 600ns; on ARM at DRAM latency FAST+FAIR is slower than FP-tree. The repo ships only FAST+FAIR, not the baseline implementations. Concurrent builds omit -O3. These are the 2018 paper's numbers; later papers such as DPTree (up to 1.82x/1.85x/2.19x faster than FAST+FAIR) and APEX beat it, so it is now a baseline rather than the fastest option.

notes: Several sub-claims were misattributed: 1.61x vs wB+-tree is ARM-only, 2.2x over B-link is FP-tree's figure, 12.5x is at 16 threads (not 8), and 20x is vs SkipList only. The default-branch (master) last commit is 2020-06-12; the record's 2021-03-12 is pushed_at, which matches a 2021-03-11 commit on the non-default issue-13 branch. Still abandoned either way. License GPL-3.0, not archived, not a fork.

tier_reason: The ICDE'13 page does show 10.4M vs 555K ops/s (18.7x) and 5.8x against BerkeleyDB, but those numbers belong to Microsoft's unreleased Win32 implementation, not this repository. The only benchmarks of this code against a recognizable incumbent are first-party screenshots in the repo's result/ folder (g++ -O3, CPU unstated), which show it slower than std::map, std::unordered_map and stx::btree. Its authors' peer-reviewed SIGMOD'18 paper likewise reports it slower than B+Tree, Masstree and ART.

corrections.claimed_speedup: This repo has no numbers against BerkeleyDB. SIGMOD'18 (OpenBw-Tree paper): 1.1-2.5x faster than the original Bw-Tree design on insert-heavy workloads and 1.1-1.4x on read-heavy ones, and faster than a lock-free SkipList. It is 'still slower than its competitors except the SkipList': ART is more than 4x faster for point lookups, and Masstree and a B+Tree with optimistic lock coupling are faster, often by about 2x. The repo's own benchmark-all screenshot (result/result-2016-07-30-2.png) gives BwTree 4.65M insert/s and 9.58M read/s vs std::map 5.91M/17.85M, std::unordered_map 15.36M/81.65M and stx::btree 10.60M/21.50M. The 18.7x (Xbox LIVE) and 5.8x (synthetic) speedups over BerkeleyDB in ICDE'13 are Microsoft's own closed-source implementation.
corrections.workload: ICDE'13 (Microsoft implementation, 8 worker threads, 8K pages): the Xbox LIVE trace is 27M get-set operations with ~94-byte alphanumeric keys, ~1200-byte payloads and a read:write ratio of about 7.5:1 (not read-only, not 8-byte integer keys); the synthetic workload uses 8-byte integer keys and payloads, a 1M-entry initial index, 42M operations and 5:1 read:write; a deduplication trace gave 8.6x. SIGMOD'18 (this code): YCSB-style Insert-only, Read-only, Read/Update and Scan/Insert workloads on random, monotonic integer and email keys, run on 2x Xeon E5-2680 v2 with g++ 5.4 and tcmalloc.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: ICDE'13 states none. SIGMOD'18: g++ 5.4 with tcmalloc. Repo result screenshots: g++ -std=c++11 -O3 (-mcx16, jemalloc via LD_PRELOAD).
corrections.hardware: ICDE'13 (Microsoft implementation): Intel Xeon W3550 @ 3.07GHz, 4 cores / 8 hyperthreads, 24GB RAM. SIGMOD'18 (this code): 2x Intel Xeon E5-2680 v2, 128GB RAM.
corrections.caveats: The Bw-Tree speedups over BerkeleyDB in ICDE'13 come from Microsoft's unreleased implementation, not this repo. The repo's README says its benchmark is 'unavailable' during a redesign. Its own first-party numbers are single-threaded, where it is slower than std::map and stx::btree. Its authors' SIGMOD'18 evaluation concludes the Bw-Tree 'still does not perform as well as other concurrent data structures that use locks'. The std::map comparison ran with g++ on Ubuntu, so libstdc++ is inferred, not explicitly stated.

notes: Reject as not-faster: the only speedup against a recognizable baseline (BerkeleyDB) belongs to different, closed code, and every benchmark of this repo's own code puts it behind std::map, stx::btree, B+Tree (OLC), Masstree and ART, ahead only of a lock-free SkipList. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 531 stars, last commit 2018-11-14, abandoned, not a fork.

tier_reason: The PVLDB'20 paper compares LB+-Tree with WB+-Tree and FP-Tree on real Optane (Cascade Lake-SP), but states no compiler or flags and no exact CPU SKU. The repo holds only lbtree-src: the fptree-src and wbtree-src directories listed in its README are absent and their Makefile targets are commented out, so the baseline benchmark code is not public. That makes it a peer-reviewed B, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: up to 1.12-2.92x speedups over state-of-the-art NVM-optimized indexes. Single-thread insertions vs WB+-Tree / FP-Tree: 70%-full leaves 1.20-1.24x / 1.12-1.21x; 100%-full leaves 2.55-2.92x / 2.31-2.45x; dense (monotonic) insertions 2.31-2.69x / 2.22-2.33x; overall 1.20-2.92x / 1.12-2.45x. With 1-16 threads: 70%-full 1.17-1.30x / 1.22-1.38x; 100%-full 2.35-2.69x / 2.10-2.53x; dense 1.90-2.38x / 1.89-2.55x. Search and deletion are similar to WB+-Tree and FP-Tree. Memcached: 1.05-1.29x over WB+-Tree and 1.06-1.22x over FP-Tree. The Get / sequential-Put / random-Put figures (1-thread 1.31-1.54x / 1.44-1.80x / 1.46-1.83x; 16-thread 1.25-1.40x / 1.35-1.64x / 1.28-1.46x) are X-Engine results against divided-skiplist, not against WB+-Tree or FP-Tree.
corrections.workload: Micro-benchmarks: bulkload 2 billion 8B-key/8B-value entries (32GB) at 70% or 100% leaf fill, then random and dense (monotonically increasing) insertions, lookups and deletions, single-threaded and 1-16 threads, with node sizes of 256B-1KB, on real Intel Optane DC PM. Also X-Engine db_bench (8B key / 20B value Get, sequential Put and random Put at 1 and 16 threads) against divided-skiplist, and Memcached mc-benchmark (500K random 20-byte string keys) against WB+-Tree and FP-Tree.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper; the repo Makefile builds with g++ -O3 -std=c++11 -pthread -mrtm -msse4.1 -mavx2 and links libpmem.
corrections.caveats: The repository has no license file (all rights reserved by default), so the code can be studied but not redistributed without asking the authors. The README lists fptree-src and wbtree-src, but they are not in the repo, so the baseline comparisons cannot be reproduced from it. Gains are insert-side only: search and delete match WB+-Tree and FP-Tree. It needs Intel RTM (TSX), PMDK and Optane PM hardware, which Intel has discontinued. The paper gives the CPU only as Cascade Lake-SP with no SKU and states no compiler or flags.

notes: The headline 1.12-2.92x is correct, but the record credited the X-Engine-vs-divided-skiplist per-operation numbers to WB+-Tree and FP-Tree, which overstates Get (search is actually on par). The default-branch last commit is 2020-09-06; the record's 2021-04-04 is pushed_at. Still abandoned. No license (null) was confirmed; the APEX baseline listing was confirmed in the APEX paper.
